The record:
Write the postmortem for the incident below.

Alert: MetricsAbsent on io-shop
What the alert said [AL1]: No metrics received from io-shop since 2026-11-12T12:34:00Z {A1} - 5m {A2} with no sample, against a scrape interval of 15 {A3} seconds. The series stopped rather than crossing a threshold, so nothing here says whether the shop is well: these minutes have no readings to judge, not readings that look bad.
Alert raised: 2026-11-12T12:39:22Z {alert_raised}
Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one. An alert rule fires; a person is paged. Argus first posted about the incident in Slack at 2026-11-12T12:39:23Z {first_told}, and the document says so already: leave that post out, and do not say that no person was told. That nobody was paged is a finding of its own.
The alert rule fires as soon as its condition holds. The alert came 2 minutes 52 seconds {beyond_accounted_for} later than the 2 minutes 30 seconds {accounted_for} accounted for by its evaluation at intervals of 1 minute {rule_evaluated_every}, an unmeasured allowance of 30 seconds {scraping_allowance} for scraping and storing its samples and the whole minute the metrics' stopping is measured to. The record does not show what took the rest.
No metrics were collected from 2026-11-12T12:34:00Z {metrics_stopped_at} (the onset, dated to its minute: a change came during that minute) onwards: the metrics had still not resumed by 2026-11-12T12:40:19Z {argus_stopped}. That is 6 minutes 19 seconds {duration} the metrics did not cover, not a stretch the service is known to have spent in trouble.
Log lines read reach into it until 2026-11-12T12:39:00Z {logs_reach_until}: [Gad41], [G46bc], [Gbac1]. They are the service's own account of that stretch: what they report there is what is known of how it was doing, and up to then the service was seen through them. The logs were read up to 2026-11-12T12:39:22Z {log_reading_ended}, when the alert was raised - nothing after that was read.
How the service did over that stretch is said by the document itself, from your answer to logs_show_serving_as_before: say nothing of it anywhere else. Where the chain's first step says nobody using the service saw anything wrong, cite those log lines for it without saying what they show.
Argus held the incident for 56 seconds {held}, until 2026-11-12T12:40:19Z {argus_stopped}. That is not how long the fault lasted, nor how long Argus went on working - leave it out of your answer.
Error rate: not measured by the metrics - none were collected after the metrics stopped; the log lines that reach into that stretch, [Gad41], [G46bc], [Gbac1], are the service's own account of it, so do not say nothing was measured; what they show is said by the document itself, from your answer to logs_show_serving_as_before.
Customer loss: none so far - the shop's takings over the incident fell short of the same hours whole weeks earlier by no more than those hours vary on their own, if at all; a lower bound, counted with the service not seen back to normal.

Log lines it read, one per message:

After they stopped: 6 {G46bc.4} occurrences in 6 {G46bc.5} minutes, 12:34–12:39 {G46bc.6}

After they stopped: 4 {Gbac1.8} occurrences in 6 {Gbac1.9} minutes, 12:34–12:39 {Gbac1.10}; # was 0.50% {Gbac1.11} to 1.50% {Gbac1.12}, typically 0.50% {Gbac1.13}, highest at 12:36 {Gbac1.14}

Candidates it considered, in the Investigator's words - name them by their labels, but cite none; what they claim is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [C1, also C2] Candidates blaming the same move of deploy/values-production.yaml, each reading it as a different kind of failure - different accounts of what it did, not one cause counted twice - each in its own words:
      C1: The deployment at 2026-11-12T12:34:18Z {C1.1} renamed every port to the platform's `<protocol>[-<purpose>]` convention in one commit. The metrics port went from `metrics` to `http-metrics`, and the scrape still selects the old name, so samples stopped. The shop itself kept serving normally. [monitoring-configuration-drift, confidence 0.82 {C1.2}, never tried: the only action that would test the candidate undoes a change that was made on purpose]
      C2: The deployment changed a configuration value that broke metrics exposure. This differs from the first account only in treating the rename as an unintended break rather than a deliberate convention. [monitoring-blind-spot, confidence 0.12 {C1.3}, never tried: the only action that would test the candidate undoes a change that was made on purpose]

Actions it took:
  - none

What each deployment it looked into changed:
  - [D1] Deployment of revision c3c36da3c66c07707f227b7e70b26813083061f3 to io-shop, compared against 2c8f7311966cf37dee314695fe0060867e1ca954 - the revision deployed before it.
      modified deploy/values-production.yaml
        @@ -31,16 +31,19 @@ autoscaling:
           scaleDownStabilizationSeconds: 0 {D1.1}
         
         # The ports the shop serves on, each selected by name rather than number.
        +#
        +# Every port is named for the protocol it carries, then what it is for:
        +# `<protocol>[-<purpose>]`. The platform's convention, applied estate-wide.
         ports:
           web:
             port: 8000 {D1.2}
        -    portName: web
        +    portName: http
           admin:
             port: 8081 {D1.3}
        -    portName: admin
        +    portName: http-admin
           metrics:
             port: 9090 {D1.4}
        -    portName: metrics
        +    portName: http-metrics
         
         # Where the rendered-summary cache lives.
         #
  - A file [D1] does not list is as it was at the revision [D1] compares against.

What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix, and what it claims is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [F1] The fault (on main, which I read; the running revision c3c36da is not in main's history, so I can't say what it held): `deploy/values-production.yaml` sets `metrics.portName: http-metrics`, but `deploy/scrape.yaml` (the ServiceMonitor) still has `endpoints[].port: metrics`. The ServiceMonitor finds its scrape endpoint by the port's name. A comment in `deploy/scrape.yaml` itself says that a name matching no port is not an error, just an empty target list, and that nothing checks the two names agree. So when the port was renamed, Prometheus had nothing to scrape. Changing the port back would reverse the platform's naming convention, so instead I changed `deploy/scrape.yaml` to select `http-metrics`, the name the values file gives the port.
      
      To stop the two drifting apart again, I added `tests/io_shop/test_scrape_config.py`. It reads both deploy files as text with simple line parsing, so it doesn't depend on a YAML library. It asserts that every `port:` named under the ServiceMonitor's `endpoints` equals `metrics.portName`. Against the code as it stood (`metrics` vs `http-metrics`) that assertion does not hold, and with this change it should. If a rename touches only one of the files in future, this test should fail in the same pull request, instead of the problem showing up as missing samples in production.
  - Say what the files Code-Fix read do, with the conditions it gives - a default as a default, never as all it does - and no wider: 'nothing in the files it read', never 'nothing in the code'. [F1] was written against main, which does not contain the revision running when the alert fired: merged, its fix changes what runs only once a deploy carries it. [F1] names revision c3c36da and [D1] is that revision's own diff - say what it shows rather than ask for it to be checked.

What ran, read at the revision running when the alert fired:
  - [S1] deploy/scrape.yaml at c3c36da
      # How the platform's Prometheus collects the shop's metrics.
      #
      # It selects the shop's Service by label, then the endpoint to scrape on that
      # Service by the port's *name* - never its number - so a port can move without
      # anything here being touched.
      #
      # The name here has to be the one `metrics.portName` in values-production.yaml
      # gives the port. Nothing checks that the two agree: a name that matches no port
      # is not an error to the operator, it is a target list with nothing in it.
      apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
      kind: ServiceMonitor
      metadata:
        name: io-shop
        labels:
          release: prometheus
      spec:
        selector:
          matchLabels:
            app: io-shop
        endpoints:
          - port: metrics
            path: /metrics
            interval: 15s {S1.1}
      
  - [S2] deploy/values-production.yaml at c3c36da
      # Deployment configuration for the io-shop account service, production.
      #
      # Rendered into the cluster as a ConfigMap and mounted into the pod, which is
      # why the service reads this file rather than being handed environment
      # variables: the values here are the deployment's, not the code's, and changing
      # one is a change to configuration that ships without the service being rebuilt.
      #
      # Owned by whoever runs the shop. Changes here go out the way any other change
      # goes out - reviewed, merged, and synced by the platform - and land without a
      # single line of io-shop's source being touched.
      
      replicas: 3 {S2.1}
      
      resources:
        memoryLimitMiB: 2048 {S2.2}
      
      # How the platform scales the shop.
      #
      # Rendered into a HorizontalPodAutoscaler, so `replicas` above is only where the
      # deployment starts: the controller decides the count from there, between the
      # floor and the ceiling here, aiming to keep each replica at the CPU target.
      #
      # `scaleDownStabilizationSeconds` is how far back the controller looks before it
      # believes a fall in load is real. Kubernetes defaults it to 300 {S2.3} - five minutes
      # of the highest recommendation it saw - because a controller acting on the
      # reading in front of it acts on a reading its own last action produced.
      autoscaling:
        minReplicas: 3 {S2.4}
        maxReplicas: 6 {S2.5}
        targetCpuPercent: 70 {S2.6}
        scaleDownStabilizationSeconds: 0 {S2.7}
      
      # The ports the shop serves on, each selected by name rather than number.
      #
      # Every port is named for the protocol it carries, then what it is for:
      # `<protocol>[-<purpose>]`. The platform's convention, applied estate-wide.
      ports:
        web:
          port: 8000 {S2.8}
          portName: http
        admin:
          port: 8081 {S2.9}
          portName: http-admin
        metrics:
          port: 9090 {S2.10}
          portName: http-metrics
      
      # Where the rendered-summary cache lives.
      #
      # The account page reads this cache before it works a shopper's spend figure
      # out, and recomputes when the cache has nothing or cannot be reached. So the
      # shop stays correct whatever is written here - it only stays *fast* while the
      # address is right.
      cache:
        host: cache.io-shop.svc.cluster.local
        port: 6380 {S2.11}
      

Action items the record already holds:
  - AI-1 (mitigate, open): Review and merge the proposed fix
PR #571 is a draft Argus opened for a person to review and merge. The record holds nothing about it after that: do not say it was reviewed, approved or merged, or that it was not - nor that the record holds nothing, which the document says itself. Nothing ran its test or its fix: say what it proposes, not that it corrects anything.
The document already states what set it off, in a section of its own: the change [P2] - suspected, not confirmed.

Cite evidence in causal_chain by its label. In a contributing factor's addressed_by, name the record's own action items that answer it, by their number; an item you propose names the factors it answers in its answers, by their labels.

Call submit_postmortem with your answer.

The document, by field:
root_cause: The deploy renamed the shop's metrics port from `metrics` to `http-metrics` in deploy/values-production.yaml, but left deploy/scrape.yaml's ServiceMonitor selecting its scrape endpoint by the old name `metrics`. The ServiceMonitor finds that endpoint by port name, and a name that matches no port gives an empty target list rather than an error, so Prometheus had nothing to scrape.
cause_in_plain_words: A planned renaming of the shop's network ports changed the name of the port the monitoring collects from, but the monitoring setup still looked for the old name, so it found nothing to collect.
still_at_risk: While the shop's metrics are not arriving, a real fault in the shop could go unnoticed by any alert that relies on those metrics.
symptom: No shopper saw anything wrong; the shop's metrics stopped arriving
causal_chain 1: Nobody using the shop saw anything wrong. What was seen instead: the shop's metrics stopped arriving from the onset minute and had not come back. (cites AL1; T5, under "What Argus did, in order"; Gad41, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; G46bc, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; Gbac1, under "Log lines it read, one per message")
causal_chain 2: Prometheus had no target to scrape. At the running revision, the shop's ServiceMonitor picks its scrape endpoint by the port name `metrics`, but the values file names the metrics port `http-metrics`. A name that matches no port gives an empty target list, not an error. (cites S1, under "What ran, read at the revision running when the alert fired"; S2, under "What ran, read at the revision running when the alert fired")
causal_chain 3: The port's name changed with the deploy of revision c3c36da at {P2.1}. That deploy renamed every port to the platform's `<protocol>[-<purpose>]` convention, including the metrics port from `metrics` to `http-metrics`. As of {T13.1}, every replica was running that revision. (cites P2, under "Changes to production it read"; D1, under "What each deployment it looked into changed"; T13, under "What Argus did, in order")
causal_chain 3 ruled_out 1: The earlier deploy of revision 2c8f731. Metrics were still arriving with it in place, through the minute before the onset. (cites P1, under "Changes to production it read"; T5, under "What Argus did, in order")
causal_chain 4: The rename broke scraping because it changed only deploy/values-production.yaml and left deploy/scrape.yaml, which has to name the same port, still selecting `metrics`. (cites D1, under "What each deployment it looked into changed"; S1, under "What ran, read at the revision running when the alert fired")
contributing_factors 1: No check was seen that the port name the ServiceMonitor selects matches the name the values file gives the metrics port. The scrape file itself says nothing checks that the two agree, and a mismatch gives an empty target list rather than an error.
contributing_factors 1 had_it_been_otherwise: A check comparing the two names would have failed the renaming change before it went out, and the metrics would not have stopped.
contributing_factors 2: The MetricsAbsent alert on io-shop paged nobody: no on-call incident was linked to it.
contributing_factors 2 had_it_been_otherwise: A paged on-call person could have taken up the escalation and the draft fix as soon as the alert fired, which would have shortened the time the shop went unmonitored.
action_items 1: Add a check to every change to deploy configuration, across all services, that fails when a ServiceMonitor endpoint names a port that the service's values file does not give any port.
action_items 2: Check the other services that the estate-wide port-naming convention renamed for ServiceMonitors that still select the old port names.
action_items 3: Route the MetricsAbsent alert for io-shop to the on-call rota so that it pages a person.
action_items 4: Find out what delayed the MetricsAbsent alert by {beyond_accounted_for} beyond what its evaluation interval and scraping allowance account for.

Not to be judged:
  - Names in braces, such as {T5.1} or {duration}, are figures code writes in from the row they name. They are not judged.
  - Action items propose what to do; they make no claim about the record.
  - Whether something went well, went wrong or was lucky is a judgement. Only a fact it states is judged, and whether a went_wrong item is one its field excludes.

Judge every claim in the document, and answer by calling judge_claims.

tools.description: Submit every claim in the document, each either as supported or as flagged. Supported: the document's own words, quoted exactly, and the record's rows that support it. Flagged: the document's own words, quoted exactly, why, and the record's rows that contradict it (none where no row speaks to it at all). Empty lists say the document makes no claim to judge.

why.description: One sentence: what the record holds instead. Never empty.
